articles.summary: If you spend an hour mowing your lawn every weekend, you probably think more about keeping the grass healthy than protecting your hearing. But that familiar engine noise can be louder than many people realize and potentially damaging to your long-term hearing. Most gas-powered lawn mowers produce between 85 and 95 decibels (dB) at the operator's ear, right at the point where prolonged exposure can begin damaging your hearing. Riding mowers, zero-turn mowers, leaf blowers, and chainsaws are often even louder. The good news is that you don't have to choose between protecting your hearing and staying aware of your surroundings. Electronic hearing protection reduces harmful noise while still allowing you to hear conversations, traffic, warning sounds, and even your favorite podcast. In this guide, we'll explain how loud common lawn equipment really is, when hearing protection is recommended, and why electronic hearing protection has become one of the best options for homeowners and lawn care professionals alike. Quick Decision If you're wondering whether you need hearing protection, here's the short answer: Equipment Wear Hearing Protection? Gas push mower Yes Riding mower Yes Zero-turn mower Yes Leaf blower Yes Chainsaw Absolutely Battery mower Usually for longer sessions or when used alongside other loud equipment If your yard work regularly includes more than just mowing, quality hearing protection is a smart investment. Quick Recommendations Push mower AXIL XCOR Pro Riding mower AXIL XCOR Pro AXIL MX Pro Zero-turn mower AXIL MX Pro Leaf blower AXIL XCOR Pro String trimmer AXIL XCOR Pro Chainsaw AXIL MX Pro How Loud Is a Lawn Mower? One of the most common questions homeowners ask is: How many decibels is a lawn mower? The answer depends on the type of mower, but most gas-powered models operate at levels where repeated exposure can contribute to permanent hearing damage. Lawn Equipment Noise Levels Equipment Typical Noise Level Hearing Protection Recommended? Battery mower 75–85 dB Sometimes Gas push mower 85–95 dB Yes Riding mower 90–100 dB Yes Zero-turn mower 90–100+ dB Yes Leaf blower 90–105 dB Yes String trimmer 90–100 dB Yes Chainsaw 105–115 dB Absolutely These numbers are approximate, but they illustrate an important point: many of the tools homeowners use every weekend operate at or above the 85 dB threshold where hearing protection becomes increasingly important during extended exposure. Keep in mind that manufacturers often measure sound several feet away from the equipment. As the operator, you're much closer to the engine, so the noise reaching your ears may be even greater. Why 85 dB Matters Noise exposure isn't just about how loud something is, it's also about how long you're exposed to it. As sound levels increase, the amount of time you can safely remain exposed decreases significantly. 85 dB8 Hours 88 dB4 Hours 91 dB2 Hours 94 dB1 Hour 97 dB30 Minutes 100 dB15 Minutes *Approximate guidance based on commonly referenced occupational noise exposure recommendations. A typical Saturday might include: 45 minutes mowing 20 minutes trimming 20 minutes blowing leaves Each task contributes to your total daily noise exposure. For professional landscapers, those hours multiply quickly, making hearing protection just as important as protective work gloves or safety glasses. Do You Really Need Hearing Protection? For most gas-powered lawn equipment, the answer is yes. Unlike broken bones or even cuts, noise-induced hearing loss happens gradually. You may not notice any changes for years, but repeated exposure to loud equipment can permanently damage the delicate structures inside your inner ear. Many people first experience: Ringing or buzzing in the ears (tinnitus) Difficulty hearing conversations in noisy environments Trouble understanding higher-pitched voices Frequently asking people to repeat themselves Once hearing damage occurs, it is irreversible. The goal isn't to avoid every loud sound, it's to reduce repeated exposure before permanent damage develops. What About Battery-Powered Mowers? Battery mowers are generally quieter than gas models, often operating between 75 and 85 dB. For a quick mow with a quieter electric mower, hearing protection may not be necessary for everyone. However, protection is still worth considering if you: Mow for an hour or more Maintain large properties Use a trimmer or leaf blower afterward Already experience tinnitus or hearing loss Being honest about this distinction builds trust. Not every mower presents the same level of risk, but many homeowners use several loud tools during the same yard work session. Why Electronic Hearing Protection Is the Best Choice Traditional foam earplugs reduce noise effectively, but they also block the sounds you often need to hear, like someone calling your name, a child playing nearby, or a vehicle pulling into the driveway. Electronic hearing protection offers a smarter solution. Using built-in microphones, it allows everyday sounds to remain audible while reducing loud, potentially harmful noise from equipment like lawn mowers, leaf blowers, and chainsaws. That means you can: Protect your hearing from prolonged engine noise Hear conversations and warning sounds Stay aware of your surroundings Listen to music or podcasts at comfortable volumes For many homeowners, this balance between protection and awareness is what finally makes hearing protection practical enough to wear every time they mow. Why Choose AXIL? Whether you prefer earbuds or earmuffs, AXIL offers electronic hearing protection designed to help reduce harmful noise without disconnecting you from the environment around you. AXIL XCOR Pro XCOR Pro is ideal for homeowners who want lightweight, comfortable protection during mowing, trimming, and leaf blowing. Its in-ear design works well with hats, sunglasses, and other outdoor gear, making it a great choice for warm-weather yard work and long mowing sessions. AXIL MX Pro MX Pro is the better option for users who prefer traditional electronic earmuffs or regularly operate louder equipment such as zero-turn mowers and chainsaws. It provides robust protection while maintaining situational awareness through electronic sound enhancement. AXIL XCOR Pro vs. MX Pro Feature XCOR Pro MX Pro Hot-weather comfort ★★★★★ ★★★☆☆ Works with hats & glasses ★★★★★ ★★★☆☆ Maximum protection ★★★★☆ ★★★★★ Chainsaw work ★★★★☆ ★★★★★ Long mowing sessions ★★★★★ ★★★★★ For most homeowners, the choice comes down to personal preference. If you like lightweight in-ear protection, XCOR Pro is an excellent fit. If you prefer the feel of electronic earmuffs or frequently use the loudest outdoor equipment, MX Pro is a strong choice. Can You Wear AirPods While Mowing? If you enjoy listening to music or podcasts while doing yard work, you may wonder whether your AirPods or noise-canceling headphones provide enough protection on their own. The short answer is no. While Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) can make a lawn mower sound quieter, it isn't the same as certified hearing protection. Consumer earbuds are designed for entertainment, not for reducing hazardous noise exposure. Another common problem is volume. As mower noise increases, many people instinctively turn their music up to hear it better. That means your ears are exposed to both engine noise and louder audio at the same time. Electronic hearing protection works differently. Instead of trying to overpower engine noise, it reduces harmful sounds first, allowing you to listen to music or podcasts at a safer, more comfortable volume. If you'd like to learn more, read our guide on Noise Cancellation vs. Hearing Protection. Other Yard Equipment That Can Damage Your Hearing Your lawn mower is only one source of noise around the yard. Many outdoor power tools operate at similar—or even higher—sound levels. Leaf Blowers Leaf blowers typically produce 90–105 dB, and backpack models can be even louder because the engine sits close to your ears. If you're blowing leaves after mowing, your total daily noise exposure increases significantly. String Trimmers and Edgers Most string trimmers operate between 90 and 100 dB. While they're smaller than lawn mowers, their higher-pitched sound can become fatiguing during extended use. Chainsaws Chainsaws commonly produce 105–115 dB, making hearing protection essential—even for quick cleanup after a storm. Riding and Zero-Turn Mowers Larger engines often mean more noise. Commercial landscapers and homeowners with large properties can spend hours at a time operating riding equipment, making consistent hearing protection especially important. The good news is that one quality set of electronic hearing protection can be used across nearly every outdoor task, from mowing and trimming to leaf blowing and chainsaw work. Frequently Asked Questions How loud is a lawn mower? Most gas-powered lawn mowers produce 85–95 dB at the operator's position. Riding and zero-turn mowers often reach 90–100 dB, while battery-powered mowers typically operate between 75 and 85 dB. Do electric lawn mowers require hearing protection? Not always. Quieter battery-powered mowers used for short periods may not require hearing protection for everyone. However, longer mowing sessions or combining multiple loud tools can increase your overall noise exposure, making hearing protection a smart choice. Can I wear AirPods while mowing? AirPods and other consumer earbuds aren't designed to protect your hearing from hazardous noise. If you want to listen to music while mowing, electronic hearing protection offers a safer alternative by reducing harmful noise while allowing you to enjoy your audio. What's the best hearing protection for mowing? Electronic hearing protection is an excellent choice because it helps reduce harmful noise while allowing you to remain aware of your surroundings. For most homeowners: AXIL XCOR Pro is ideal if you prefer lightweight electronic earbuds. AXIL MX Pro is a great option if you want the feel and protection of electronic earmuffs. Do I need hearing protection for a leaf blower? Yes. Most leaf blowers produce 90–105 dB, which is loud enough that hearing protection is recommended, especially during extended use or when combined with other outdoor power equipment. Protect Your Hearing Every Time You Mow Mowing the lawn may feel like a routine weekend chore, but the noise generated by lawn equipment can add up over time. Gas-powered mowers, leaf blowers, trimmers, and chainsaws all operate at levels capable of contributing to permanent hearing damage with repeated exposure. The good news is that protecting your hearing doesn't have to mean shutting yourself off from the world around you. Electronic hearing protection helps reduce harmful noise while allowing you to stay aware of your surroundings, communicate with others, and even enjoy music or podcasts during yard work. Whether you're maintaining your own lawn or spending every day on a landscaping crew, wearing hearing protection is one of the simplest steps you can take to protect your long-term hearing health. If you're ready to upgrade your yard work routine, explore AXIL XCOR Pro electronic earbuds for lightweight comfort or AXIL MX Pro electronic earmuffs for maximum protection around louder equipment. Both are designed to help you work more comfortably while protecting one of your most valuable senses. articles.summary: People starting a GLP-1 medication often hope to feel a little more control over their day-to-day health through appetite support, metabolic changes, and meaningful weight progress. So when their hair begins to shed, it can feel like progress in one area has brought a new worry somewhere else. Can GLP-1 medications cause hair loss? Or is the shedding connected to the body changes that can happen during treatment? In many cases, hair shedding during a GLP-1 routine may be related to weight change, appetite shifts, nutrition gaps, and physical stress on the body rather than direct follicle injury. When the body changes quickly, more hairs can move into the resting phase, creating a temporary shedding condition called telogen effluvium. The good news is that resting hair follicles are not permanently damaged follicles. GLP-1-related hair shedding can feel sudden, but the hair cycle can recover as weight change slows, nutrition becomes more consistent, and the scalp gets steady care. Why GLP-1 Hair Loss Gets Discussed GLP-1 medications are often discussed alongside hair shedding because they can influence appetite, portion size, eating patterns, and weight change. That does not automatically mean the medication is directly damaging the hair follicle. For many people, the more helpful question is: what changed in the body around the time shedding started? Hair shedding may become more noticeable when several changes happen at once: Possible Change During a GLP-1 Routine Why It May Affect Hair Lower appetite Smaller meals may make it harder to get enough protein and key nutrients. Faster weight change Rapid body change can act as a stress signal to the hair cycle. Skipped meals Fewer meals can mean fewer chances to support hair-building nutrition. Lower protein intake Hair depends on steady amino acids to support the next growth cycle. Nutrient gaps Iron, zinc, vitamin D, B vitamins, and healthy fats all play a role in hair and scalp health. Overlapping triggers Stress, illness, thyroid changes, postpartum changes, menopause, or existing thinning can make shedding more visible. So if you are wondering whether GLP-1 medications can cause hair loss, the answer is usually more nuanced than a simple yes or no. The hair conversation often comes back to how your body responds to changes in appetite, weight, nutrition, stress, and overall health while using a GLP-1 medication. Why Hair Loss Can Happen During a GLP-1 Routine When appetite drops, meals often get smaller. When weight changes quickly, the body has more to adapt to. When protein, iron, vitamin D, B vitamins, zinc, or healthy fats become harder to get consistently, the hair cycle can respond. articles.summary: You're committed to making healthy changes to yourself. You started a GLP-1 medication, your appetite changed, the weight began to move, but then a few months later, your hair starts showing up everywhere: in the shower, in your brush, and on your pillow. That kind of shedding can feel personal, especially when you are doing something positive for your health. So it is natural to ask: do GLP-1 medications cause hair loss? The good news is that current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly damage hair follicles. Instead, rapid weight loss, lower food intake, and nutrient changes can place stress on the body, which may push more hairs into the resting phase. Doctors often evaluate this kind of diffuse shedding as possible telogen effluvium, a common and usually temporary type of shedding that can happen after major changes like weight loss, illness, surgery, stress, or hormonal changes. This kind of shedding is often a sign that your body and scalp need support, not a sign that your hair is gone for good. GLP-1 Hair Loss Is Usually Linked to Weight Loss, Not Follicle Damage GLP-1 medications are used to support blood sugar management, weight management, and certain cardiometabolic health goals, depending on the specific prescription and patient need. Hair loss is not commonly framed as direct follicle damage in this context, although some patients still report shedding during a GLP-1 routine. That can feel confusing. Your experience can still be real even when hair loss is not considered a common listed side effect for every GLP-1 medication. More likely, the link between GLP-1 medications and hair shedding is indirect. When someone eats less, loses weight quickly, or gets less protein and key nutrients during treatment, the body may respond to that change as stress. More hairs can move into the resting phase, and a few months later, those resting hairs may shed at the same time. GLP-1 Medications Do Not Appear to Attack Hair Follicles Directly Current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly damage the follicle. In many cases, the follicle is still active beneath the surface. It may simply be resting. That's important because resting follicles can often return to the growth phase once the body stabilizes. Most GLP-1-Related Shedding Is Temporary Hair shedding can feel alarming, but it does not automatically mean permanent hair loss. Many cases that fit telogen effluvium improve once the trigger settles and the body receives consistent support. Talk with your prescribing clinician before changing any GLP-1 medication. Then review your nutrition, watch for other symptoms, and support your scalp with a gentle, consistent routine. How Weight Loss on GLP-1 Medications Can Affect the Hair Cycle Hair follicles are sensitive to change. They rely on steady nutrition, energy, and internal balance to keep producing strong, healthy-looking strands. Telogen effluvium happens when more hairs than usual move into the resting phase of the hair cycle. This can happen after weight loss, illness, surgery, stress, hormonal changes, medication changes, or a major diet change. With GLP-1 medications, the trigger may be the change happening around treatment: less food, faster weight loss, and lower intake of nutrients that help support normal hair growth. Here is the simple version: Appetite drops or weight changes quickly. The body experiences internal stress. More follicles move into the resting phase. Two to four months later, those resting hairs shed together. Lower Appetite Can Mean Lower Hair-Supportive Nutrition Many people eat less during GLP-1-supported weight loss, especially when fullness comes sooner or meals become smaller. When food intake drops sharply, protein and micronutrient intake may drop too. Hair production is an active biological process. Your follicles need consistent support from nutrients like protein, iron, B vitamins, vitamin D, and zinc. Nutrient gaps do not cause every case of hair loss, but low protein intake, low iron stores, and certain vitamin or mineral deficiencies may contribute to shedding for some people. Nutrient Why Hair May Need It What You Should Do Protein Supports keratin production Ask about daily protein targets Iron / Ferritin Supports oxygen transport and growth processes Discuss labs if hair shedding is heavy B12 Supports red blood cell and nerve function Discuss testing if intake is low or fatigue is present Vitamin D Associated with hair and immune function Ask about testing if deficiency risk is high Zinc Supports tissue repair and growth Avoid high-dose supplementation without guidance A clinician can help you decide whether lab testing makes sense. GLP-1 Hair Loss Often Shows Up Months Later One of the most confusing parts of GLP-1-related hair loss is the timing. You may feel fine at first. Your appetite changes. Your weight begins to move. Then, a few months later, the hair shedding becomes hard to miss. Some people may also notice a wider-looking part line or more visible thinning around the crown, especially in certain lighting. Signs Your Shedding May Fit Telogen Effluvium Shedding started 2 to 4 months after weight loss or appetite change. Hair falls from across the scalp rather than one patch. More strands appear in the shower, brush, or pillow. The scalp does not show scarring, pain, or severe inflammation. The part line or ponytail looks thinner than usual. If this sounds familiar, try not to panic. Look at the full picture: how quickly your weight changed, whether your protein intake dropped, whether nutrient levels may be low, and whether stress, styling habits, or hormonal changes may also be contributing. Your hair may be responding to a season of change. With the right support, your body and scalp can have a steadier foundation while the hair cycle recovers. Ozempic Hair Loss in Women: Hormones, Nutrition, and Scalp Support For many women, hair changes feel personal right away. A wider part line, a thinner ponytail, or more visible scalp at the crown can affect how you feel when you look in the mirror, even if the shedding is temporary. If you are trying to understand hair loss while taking a GLP-1 medication, it helps to look at the full picture. For women, hair shedding may be connected to weight changes, nutrition, hormones, stress, scalp health, or a combination of factors. Common overlapping triggers can include: Iron deficiency Thyroid changes Postpartum hair changes Perimenopause or menopause PCOS Stress Low protein intake Androgen-related thinning Tight hairstyles, extensions, or tension at the scalp Talk with a doctor or dermatologist if heavy hair shedding comes with fatigue, dizziness, brittle nails, irregular periods, cold intolerance, scalp pain, scaling, or patchy hair loss. Those signs may point to something beyond temporary shedding. Hair shedding is not your fault. A steady plan can support your body, protect your scalp, and give fragile hair the gentler care it needs while the hair cycle resets. How Long It Takes Hair to Recover After GLP-1 Shedding The hardest part of GLP-1-related hair shedding is that it rarely follows the timeline you expect. You may already feel settled into your medication routine when the hair shedding suddenly becomes noticeable. The encouraging part is that this type of shedding is often temporary. Once weight loss slows, nutrition becomes more consistent, and the body feels less stressed, the hair cycle can begin to steady itself. Shedding may improve before full density returns, so patience matters. Phase Possible Timing What You May Notice Trigger Weeks 1 to 12 Appetite drops, weight changes, or nutrient intake changes Onset Months 2 to 4 More hair appears in the shower, brush, or pillow Peak Months 4 to 6 The part line, crown, or ponytail may look thinner Stabilization Months 6 to 9 Shedding may slow as weight and nutrition stabilize Regrowth Months 9 to 12+ Short new hairs may appear, and density may gradually improve Visible recovery takes time because hair grows slowly. Even after shedding slows, it may take several months for new growth to make hair feel fuller again. Diffuse shedding can fit telogen effluvium, but patchy loss, scalp pain, scaling, scarring, or shedding that lasts beyond six months should be reviewed by a medical professional. How to Care for Your Hair and Scalp While Taking GLP-1 Medications When hair shedding feels sudden, it is completely understandable to try a proactive approach to resolve it, especially when your hair feels more fragile than usual. A supportive approach starts with a steady plan: help your body get the nutrients it needs, protect your scalp, and reduce unnecessary stress on shedding-prone hair. No shampoo, supplement, or scalp treatment can promise to stop GLP-1-related shedding overnight. But a thoughtful routine can help you care for your scalp, reduce visible breakage, and support healthier-looking hair while the hair cycle stabilizes. Start With the Nutrients Your Hair Depends On Hair growth is an active process, so your body needs consistent support while weight and appetite are changing. If shedding feels heavy or prolonged, ask your clinician whether it makes sense to review protein intake, iron and ferritin, vitamin B12, vitamin D, zinc, thyroid function, weight-loss speed, and other medications or health changes. This matters even more if shedding comes with fatigue, dizziness, brittle nails, cold intolerance, or other symptoms. Keep Your Scalp Routine Gentle and Consistent GLP-1-related shedding often begins inside the body, but your daily hair-care routine happens at the scalp. Scalp care cannot replace nutrition or medical guidance. Still, a gentle routine can help create a cleaner, more balanced environment for healthier-looking hair while your body adjusts. A scalp-supportive routine can help remove buildup without over-stripping, keep the scalp feeling clean, support the look and feel of stronger hair, reduce visible breakage, and limit stress from harsh cleansing, tight styles, or aggressive brushing. Make Small, Steady Changes Instead of Starting Over When hair is shedding, it can be tempting to try every product, supplement, or styling change at once. Too many changes can make it harder to know what is helping. A simpler routine is often better. Focus on internal support, gentle scalp care, low-tension styling, and medical guidance when needed. That daily routine can become a steady, supportive step while your body adjusts. Reviv3 does not replace medical care, nutrition support, lab testing, or guidance from your GLP-1 prescriber. Instead, Reviv3 helps you build a simple scalp-first routine that supports cleaner roots, healthier-looking strands, and a more consistent approach to hair care during shedding. For hair that already feels fragile, a clean scalp environment can make the rest of your routine feel lighter and easier to maintain. Shop PREP → PRIME PRIME Moisture+ Conditioner supports hair that feels dry, delicate, or harder to manage during active shedding. Softer, more manageable hair can help reduce unnecessary stress from brushing, detangling, and styling. Shop PRIME → TREAT TREAT Micro-Active3 Treatment is the leave-in scalp step that fits Reviv3's scalp-first approach. Its peptide-forward, botanical-based formula supports the scalp environment and supports the look and feel of stronger, fuller hair with consistent use. Shop TREAT → BOOST BOOST Biotin Cellular Complex can complement a hair-supportive wellness routine for readers who want targeted support. Shop BOOST → Reviv3 can support scalp health, help strengthen the look and feel of hair, and help reduce visible breakage. GLP-1 Hair Loss Mistakes That Can Make Shedding Feel Worse GLP-1 hair loss can feel urgent, but sudden medication changes, crash dieting, over-supplementing, and aggressive hair routines can add more stress to an already sensitive hair cycle. Common Mistake Better Move Stopping GLP-1 medication suddenly Call your prescriber first Eating too little protein Ask about a realistic daily protein target Trying every hair product at once Build one consistent scalp-care routine Ignoring patchy or painful loss See a dermatologist Mega-dosing supplements Ask about labs and safe dosing Do not stop a GLP-1 medication without medical guidance. Medication decisions should consider blood sugar management, weight-management goals, cardiovascular risk, kidney health, and your overall medical history. Avoid crash dieting while your appetite is already lower. Very low food intake can add to the body stress that may contribute to shedding, especially if protein and key nutrients drop too quickly. Be careful with supplements, too. More is not always better. High-dose iron, zinc, vitamin D, or other hair supplements may be unnecessary or unsafe without lab guidance. When to See a Doctor About GLP-1 Hair Loss Many cases of GLP-1-related shedding are temporary, but you should not have to guess your way through it. If something feels unusual, a clinician can help you understand whether the shedding fits telogen effluvium or whether another factor may be involved. Talk to a medical professional if you notice: Patchy hair loss Scalp pain, redness, scaling, or scarring Shedding that lasts longer than six months Heavy shedding with fatigue or dizziness Brittle nails, cold intolerance, or heavy periods Signs of infection or inflammation Sudden worsening of hair density Patchy hair loss may point to alopecia areata, fungal infection, traction alopecia, or another scalp condition that needs a closer look. Diffuse shedding with fatigue, dizziness, or brittle nails may also be a reason to ask about lab testing for nutrient deficiencies, thyroid changes, or anemia. Common Questions About GLP-1 Hair Loss Do GLP-1 Medications Cause Hair Loss? Current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly target or damage hair follicles. However, GLP-1 medications may contribute to shedding indirectly when rapid weight loss, reduced food intake, or nutrient changes place stress on the body. Diffuse shedding in this context is often evaluated as possible telogen effluvium. Is Hair Loss a Side Effect of GLP-1 Medications? Hair loss is not listed as a common side effect for every GLP-1 medication. Still, some patients and clinicians report shedding in GLP-1 weight-loss contexts. Your shedding can be real even if it is not considered a common listed side effect. Can GLP-1 Medications Cause Hair Loss? GLP-1 medications may be associated with hair shedding in some patients, especially when weight changes happen quickly. The risk appears to be connected to weight-loss speed, lower food intake, nutrition changes, and individual health factors rather than direct follicle damage. How Long Does GLP-1 Hair Loss Last? GLP-1-related shedding may last several months, especially if weight loss is still happening quickly or nutrition remains low. Many cases that fit telogen effluvium improve once the body stabilizes, but visible regrowth often takes longer than the shedding itself. Will Hair Grow Back After GLP-1 Hair Loss? Hair often improves after telogen effluvium because the follicles are usually resting rather than permanently destroyed. Give the hair cycle time, and seek medical guidance if shedding is severe, patchy, painful, or lasts longer than expected. How Can Women Stop Hair Loss From GLP-1 Medications? Women can support hair during a GLP-1 routine by reviewing protein intake, asking a clinician about iron, thyroid, B12, vitamin D, or other relevant labs, reducing styling stress, and using a consistent scalp-care routine. Women should not stop a GLP-1 medication without guidance from their prescribing clinician. Can You Prevent Hair Loss While Taking GLP-1 Medications? You may be able to lower the risk of shedding by avoiding crash dieting, maintaining enough protein, asking about nutrient labs when appropriate, losing weight at a medically guided pace, and supporting scalp health consistently. GLP-1 Shedding Can Improve With Time, Nutrition, and Scalp Care GLP-1 hair loss can feel frustrating, especially when the shedding seems to appear out of nowhere. In many cases, it is more understandable than it first feels. Current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly damage hair follicles. More often, shedding is linked to the changes happening around weight loss and the stress those changes can place on the body. When more hairs move into the resting phase, visible shedding can show up a few months later. Steady support makes a meaningful difference. Your body may simply be adapting while your meals have become smaller. Hair is sensitive to overall nourishment. When appetite drops, certain nutrients can become easier to miss, even when you are still making healthy choices. How Reduced Appetite Can Leave Hair-Supporting Nutrients Behind GLP-1 medications can help you feel full sooner, which often means you eat less throughout the day. For your hair, a smaller appetite becomes important when smaller meals no longer provide enough protein, iron, zinc, B vitamins, vitamin D, and other nutrients your body uses to support healthy hair. Hair shedding has been reported during GLP-1 treatment, but the connection is often tied to weight change, lower intake, or other body stressors rather than the medication directly attacking hair. Your body is smart about priorities. During rapid weight loss, lower intake, nausea, or skipped meals, it may direct energy and nutrients toward the functions it needs most. Hair may be one place where that change becomes noticeable because follicles are sensitive to nutrition, stress, and the body's daily rhythm. Targeted supplements may be helpful when food intake or bloodwork points to a real nutrient gap. A better starting point is understanding what your hair may be missing, what your body may need, and how to support both your nutrition and scalp with consistency. Smaller Meals Can Still Miss Key Nutrients Healthy choices can still fall short when portions become much smaller. You may be eating cleaner, lighter, or more intentionally, while your total nutrient intake still drops. A fruit breakfast may feel refreshing, but it may not give your body enough protein. A small salad may feel balanced, but it may not provide enough iron, zinc, B12, or vitamin D. During a GLP-1 routine, steady nutrient coverage matters more than perfect eating. Hair Support Works Best From the Inside and the Scalp Up Nutrition supports the body from within. Scalp care supports the environment where hair grows. Food, testing, and clinician guidance help you understand your internal nutrient needs. A scalp-first routine helps care for the outside foundation, especially when shedding has made your hair feel more fragile or your scalp needs extra attention. Reviv3 fits into this routine from the scalp side. Its clean, targeted system helps refresh the scalp, support comfort, and create a healthier-feeling foundation for stronger-looking hair while your body adjusts to a new weight-loss rhythm. 01 Protein Gives Hair the Building Blocks It Needs to Stay Strong Protein matters because hair is made mostly of keratin. When your appetite gets smaller on a GLP-1 medication, protein can become harder to get enough of. It may also be one of the first things to fall off the plate because protein-rich foods often feel more filling than fruit, crackers, soup, or lighter meals. That matters for your hair because protein provides amino acids, the raw materials your body uses for normal tissue maintenance. When intake stays too low, your body may have less support available for non-essential tissues like hair. Protein deficiency hair loss can happen during periods of rapid weight loss or reduced intake. You do not need to eat perfectly. You do need enough building blocks to support your hair, muscles, energy, and recovery while your routine changes. Start With Protein Before Your Appetite Runs Out A protein-first habit can make smaller meals work harder for you. When you know you may not finish a full plate, eat the protein portion first, then move to the rest of the meal. Simple protein-first ideas include: Eggs before toast Greek yogurt before fruit Chicken, fish, tofu, or lean meat before rice or pasta Cottage cheese or a protein smoothie when a full meal feels difficult Lentils, beans, or tempeh for plant-forward meals Protein first does not mean protein only. It simply gives your hair and body the raw materials they need before fullness sets in. 02 Iron Helps Hair Follicles Get the Oxygen They Need Iron plays a subtle but important role in hair health. It helps red blood cells move oxygen through the body, including to the active tissues that support the hair cycle. When iron stores run low, follicles may not get the same steady support they need to stay in rhythm. Ferritin is the storage form of iron, and it often comes up when shedding becomes noticeable. You can have low iron stores before obvious anemia shows up, which is why ferritin testing can be helpful for some people. This may be worth discussing if you have heavy periods, eat little or no meat, follow a vegetarian or vegan diet, or find yourself eating much smaller meals on a GLP-1 routine. Ask About Ferritin Before Guessing With Iron Hair shedding alone cannot tell you whether your iron is low. If you are noticing more hair in your brush, shower, or on your pillow, ask a clinician whether ferritin testing and a complete blood count make sense. Iron is essential, but it is not a nutrient to supplement blindly. Too much iron can be harmful, so bloodwork should guide the next step. Choose Iron-Rich Foods That Work With Smaller Meals Iron-rich foods can fit into a GLP-1 routine without requiring a large plate. Focus on nutrient-dense options you can eat consistently, even when your appetite is lower. Lean red meat Poultry Seafood Lentils Beans Spinach Pumpkin seeds Iron-fortified cereals Plant-based iron sources pair well with vitamin C foods like citrus, strawberries, bell peppers, tomatoes, or broccoli. That pairing can help your body absorb non-heme iron more effectively. 03 Zinc Helps Support the Repair Work Hair Follicles Need Zinc does a lot of behind-the-scenes work for hair health. It supports cell repair, protein synthesis, and normal follicle function, which makes it an important mineral for hair that is already under stress from rapid weight change or lower food intake. During a GLP-1 routine, zinc can become easier to miss if smaller meals mean you are eating less meat, seafood, legumes, seeds, nuts, or dairy. That does not mean everyone needs a standalone zinc supplement. It means zinc deserves a steady place in the larger hair-support plan. Add Zinc in Small, Nutrient-Dense Ways You do not need a large meal to bring more zinc into your routine. Small, protein-forward foods can help support zinc intake when your appetite is lower. Oysters & shellfish Beef Turkey Pumpkin seeds Chickpeas Lentils Cashews Yogurt Small additions can build over time. Try pumpkin seeds on Greek yogurt, chickpeas in a small bowl, cashews as a snack, or turkey as part of a protein-first meal. Keep Zinc Support Balanced Zinc supports hair health best when it works alongside the rest of your nutrient foundation: protein, iron, B vitamins, vitamin D, enough calories, and consistent scalp care. It is also a mineral where more is not always better. High-dose zinc can interfere with copper absorption, so avoid stacking multiple zinc-heavy supplements unless a healthcare provider recommends it. Think steady coverage rather than megadosing. Zinc can be helpful when intake is low, but it works best as one part of a balanced hair wellness routine. 04 B Vitamins Help Your Body Turn Food Into Hair Support B vitamins help power your daily energy system. They help your body break down food and use it for normal functions, including the processes that keep hair follicles active and healthy. During a GLP-1 routine, B vitamins can become easier to miss when appetite is lower or meals become more repetitive. If you are eating fewer animal foods, fewer fortified foods, or less variety overall, your intake of biotin, B12, and other B vitamins may need a closer look. Biotin gets a lot of attention in hair conversations, and it does belong here. Biotin can support hair health when intake is low or deficiency is possible. Taking more biotin does not automatically mean more hair growth, especially if your levels are already normal. Biotin Can Help When Your Body Is Running Low Biotin supports normal metabolism and is commonly associated with hair, skin, and nails. It can be a useful part of a hair-support routine when appetite drops, food variety becomes limited, or a deficiency is possible. Keep expectations realistic. Biotin is not a shortcut for hair shedding during a GLP-1 routine. It works best as one part of a bigger routine that includes enough protein, minerals, calories, scalp care, and time for the hair cycle to respond. B12 Is Worth Watching When Meals Get Smaller Vitamin B12 is found mostly in animal foods like meat, fish, eggs, and dairy. If those foods are showing up less often in your routine, it may be worth asking a clinician whether B12 testing makes sense. B12 is especially worth discussing if shedding appears alongside fatigue, weakness, numbness, tingling, or brain fog. Those symptoms can have many possible causes, so testing is a clearer next step than guessing. Tell Your Clinician About Biotin Before Lab Work High-dose biotin can interfere with certain blood tests, including some hormone-related tests. If you take biotin, let your healthcare provider know before bloodwork so your results can be interpreted accurately. Research notes that biotin above recommended amounts may cause false results in some lab tests, including tests that measure certain hormones such as thyroid hormone. B vitamin-rich foods include: Eggs Salmon Tuna Beef Dairy Fortified nutritional yeast Fortified cereals Legumes Leafy greens 05 Vitamin D Supports Hair, Skin, and Scalp Health Vitamin D plays a meaningful role in overall skin and immune health. It may also be involved in follicle-related processes, which makes it worth discussing when your hair is already responding to changes in weight, appetite, or nutrition. A GLP-1 medication does not automatically cause vitamin D deficiency. But when meals get smaller or food variety narrows, vitamin D can become harder to maintain for some people, especially if sun exposure is limited. Vitamin D is not a guaranteed fix for shedding. It is one nutrient worth checking when your intake, lifestyle, or health history suggests your body may need extra support. Choose Vitamin D Foods When Your Plate Is Smaller Vitamin D can be harder to get from food alone, but a few nutrient-dense choices can help support daily intake. Salmon Sardines Egg yolks Fortified milk Fortified plant milks Fortified cereals Food is only one part of the vitamin D picture. Sun exposure, skin tone, location, age, sunscreen habits, and health history can all affect your levels. Use Testing to Take the Guesswork Out of Vitamin D If you have limited sun exposure, a known deficiency, darker skin, a restrictive diet, or persistent shedding, ask a clinician whether vitamin D testing makes sense. If your levels are low, a healthcare provider can recommend a dose and timeline that fits your body. That way, your routine feels more personal, more informed, and less like a guessing game. When Appetite Is Low, Hair Support Needs a Smarter Routine A nutrient list can help you understand what your hair needs. A routine helps you actually support it. You do not need to turn every meal into a math problem. Make smaller meals work harder, use testing when guesswork is not enough, and care for the scalp while your body adjusts to a new weight-loss rhythm. Make Smaller Meals Work Harder for Your Hair When appetite is low, start with the nutrients that give your body the most support first. Eat protein first at meals. Add iron- and zinc-rich foods throughout the week. Pair plant-based iron with vitamin C foods. Keep meals consistent, even when portions are small. Ask about testing before adding iron, high-dose vitamin D, or B12. Tell your clinician about biotin before lab work. Support the scalp with a consistent, gentle routine. Support the Scalp While Your Body Adjusts Nutrition supports your body from within. Reviv3 supports the scalp side of the routine, where stronger-looking hair begins. Reviv3's scalp-first system is designed to help care for the environment where hair grows while your body adapts to changes in appetite, weight, and nutrition. PREP PREP Cleanser helps remove buildup so the scalp feels clean, refreshed, and ready for the rest of the routine. Shop PREP → PRIME PRIME Conditioner helps support softness, hydration, shine, and scalp comfort. Shop PRIME → TREAT TREAT Micro-Activ3 Treatment supports the scalp with a leave-in peptide and botanical treatment designed for ongoing scalp care. Shop TREAT → BOOST BOOST Biotin Cellular Complex is applied to visibly thinning areas and features topical biotin-based peptides, botanical extracts, caffeine, and a chelated vitamin complex. Shop BOOST → Start with steady nutrition. Then support the scalp with a routine designed for the place where healthier-looking hair begins. What to Know About GLP-1 Hair Shedding and Supplements What vitamins should I prioritize for hair shedding on GLP-1 medications? If your appetite has dropped while taking a GLP-1 medication, start with the nutrients your hair depends on most: protein, iron, zinc, B vitamins, and vitamin D. A clinician can also help you decide whether bloodwork makes sense. Ferritin, B12, vitamin D, thyroid markers, and a complete blood count may be worth discussing if shedding is noticeable or persistent. Can supplements stop GLP-1 hair shedding? Supplements may help when shedding is connected to a nutrient gap, but they are not a guaranteed fix for every type of hair loss. Hair shedding while taking GLP-1 medications can also be influenced by rapid weight loss, stress, hormones, thyroid changes, genetics, medications, and scalp health. A steady approach often works best: enough food, the right testing, targeted supplements when needed, and a scalp-care routine that supports the environment where hair grows. Does biotin help with GLP-1 hair shedding? Biotin may support hair health when biotin intake is low or deficiency is possible. More biotin does not automatically mean more hair growth if your levels are already normal. If you take biotin, tell your clinician before bloodwork. High-dose biotin can interfere with certain lab tests, so your provider should know what you are taking before results are interpreted. Is protein deficiency hair loss common during weight loss? Protein deficiency can contribute to shedding when calorie intake and protein intake stay too low. This can happen during weight loss, especially when appetite changes make protein-rich foods harder to finish. If you are taking a GLP-1 medication, a protein-first habit can help. Eat the protein portion of your meal before your appetite runs out, and ask a clinician or dietitian for a protein target that fits your body and health needs. Should I get bloodwork checked for GLP-1 hair shedding? Bloodwork may be helpful if shedding is noticeable, persistent, or paired with fatigue, weakness, dizziness, heavy periods, restrictive eating, numbness, or brain fog. Ask your clinician whether ferritin, B12, vitamin D, thyroid markers, and a complete blood count make sense for you. Testing can help you move from guessing to a more personalized support plan. What is the best supplement for hair shedding on GLP-1 medications? There may not be one best supplement for everyone. The right support depends on your diet, bloodwork, health history, and medication plan. If smaller meals are making nutrient intake harder, a targeted supplement may help fill certain gaps, but iron, B12, and vitamin D are best guided by testing. It also helps to remember that supplements support one side of the routine. Scalp care supports the other. How long does GLP-1 hair shedding last? Hair shedding during a GLP-1 routine may improve once weight loss stabilizes, nutrient intake becomes more consistent, and other possible triggers are addressed. The timeline can vary because the hair cycle moves slowly. If shedding is severe, patchy, sudden, or does not improve, speak with a healthcare provider or dermatologist. Your GLP-1 Hair Routine Can Start With One Steady Step Hair shedding during a GLP-1 routine can feel unsettling, especially when your appetite, body, and daily routine are already changing. You do not have to respond with panic or a shelf full of guesswork. Start with one steady step: support the nutrients your hair depends on most. Smaller meals can make protein, iron, zinc, B vitamins, and vitamin D easier to miss, so food comes first, testing helps when something feels off, and supplements should match what your body actually needs. Then care for the scalp with the same consistency. Nutrition supports your hair from within, while Reviv3's scalp-first system helps care for the environment where healthier-looking hair begins. For a more complete routine, many customers pair the Reviv3 haircare regimen with hair regrowth gummies like FOLLY, so they can support their hair journey from the outside and the inside. Support your hair from the inside and the scalp up. Explore Reviv3's scalp-first routine or take the Hair Quiz to find the right support for your hair concerns.

articles.summary: A short training session or recreational trip to an indoor range without effective and properly worn ear protection can easily cause permanent or even short-term hearing damage. Firearms produce impulse noise between 140 and 175 decibels, far exceeding the 85 dB threshold considered safe for human hearing. Whether you're a first-time range visitor, a recreational/competitive shooter, or training in a tactical environment, choosing the correct hearing protection is critical. What makes hearing protection critical can require a substantial amount of research. The good news? There are options for every scenario including, from inexpensive foam ear plugs to advanced electronic systems that let you hear conversations while blocking hazardous noise levels. In this guide, we'll take a deep dive into the best ear protection for shooting, explain how much you actually need, and assist in choosing the right setup for your specific use case. How Loud Is Shooting? (Why This Matters) Gunfire is not just loud, it can be dangerously loud and harmful to your ears. Here's a breakdown of common firearm noise levels: ~125 dB Suppressed 9mm Most common defensive handgun cartridge for law enforcement, military, and civilian self defense. ~140 dB .22 LR Rifle Extremely common for recreational shooting (plinking). ~165 dB .223/5.56 AR-15 Most common sporting rifle for match and recreational shooting as well as varmint hunting. ~165 dB 12-Gauge Shotgun Law enforcement and sporting, hunting, and home defense applications. ~170 dB .308 Rifle Most popular cartridge for hunting white tail deer, with military and law enforcement applications. Anything above 140 dB can cause immediate, irreversible hearing damage. Indoor ranges are even worse due to sound reflecting off of walls, increasing noise levels by an additional 5–10 dB, making proper protection even more critical, particularly with rifles and larger calibers. Types of Ear Protection for Shooting Foam Ear Plugs NRR 28–33 28–33. They are economical and widely available, making them a great option for beginners or as a backup. They are worn by being inserted into the ear canal where they expand and block all sound, including important range commands and other cues — a safety and awareness consideration when in a stall with limited peripheral vision. Shop Foam Plugs → Reusable Ear Plugs NRR 22–28 A step up in durability and comfort with generally higher quality than standard foam plugs. They're ideal for plinkers on a budget, but like foam plugs, they still block out all ambient sound, restricting awareness and communication. Shop Reusable Plugs → Passive Ear Muffs NRR 22–30 Passive ear muffs provide 22–30 NRR and are faster and easier to put on and take off, making them popular for beginners and casual shooters. The downside is bulk and lack of sound awareness — not optimal for communication, and may cause issues when shouldering a long gun properly. Shop Passive Muffs → Electronic Ear Muffs NRR 22–28 Electronic muffs combine protection with awareness for optimal communication in the field and on the range. They block harmful noise while amplifying safe sounds. Best for instructors, frequent shooters, and range environments like competition or training. Shop Electronic Muffs → Electronic In-Ear NRR 18–25 Electronic ear plugs are the newest and most advanced option available and also come with the most features. Bluetooth, directional hearing, low-profile fit. Ideal for competition shooters and tactical use where mobility and spatial awareness are critical. Shop Electronic In-Ear → Best Ear Protection by Shooting Context Indoor Range Foam plugs + electronic muffs The most hazardous environment due to sound reflection. Doubling up is strongly recommended. Even if muffs are knocked off during training, plugs provide a last line of defense. Outdoor Range Electronic muffs or plugs NRR 22+ Sound dissipates more naturally, but gunshot reports remain potentially damaging. Electronic options give protection while maintaining communication and spatial awareness. Competition Shooting Electronic in-ear plugs Speed and awareness are top priorities. Rapid physical movement and sweat moisture are additional factors. Electronic in-ear provides secure fit, low profile, and clear hearing of range officer commands. Tactical / LE Training Electronic in-ear with Bluetooth / comms Communication and situational awareness are critical. These systems allow seamless team coordination while protecting hearing and enabling directional awareness for early threat detection. NRR Ratings Explained — How Much Protection Do You Actually Need? The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) tells you how much sound a device can block, but real-world performance can be lower than advertised. NRR Rating Formula Real-World Reduction NRR 22 (22 – 7) ÷ 2 ~7.5 dB NRR 25 (25 – 7) ÷ 2 ~9 dB NRR 28 (28 – 7) ÷ 2 ~10.5 dB NRR 33 (33 – 7) ÷ 2 ~13 dB This is why higher NRR and sometimes doubling up can be necessary and a best practice. Doubling Up — When and How to Wear Plugs + Muffs Doubling up means wearing ear plugs + ear muffs together. When to Do It Indoor ranges Shooting high-caliber rifles Long shooting sessions Important: NRR values don't stack directly. Instead, add about +5 dB to the higher-rated protection. Also consider that hearing protection can be uncomfortable and there is an adjustment period when someone is new to shooting. New shooters should make it a point to wear hearing protection before going to the range to get used to the slight discomfort in a non-hazardous noise environment. FAQ What is the best ear protection for shooting? This depends greatly on the environment. Indoor ranges require maximum protection (doubling up), while outdoor and competition shooting benefit from electronic options. Hearing protection should be tested off the range beforehand and phased into gradually, starting with smaller caliber firearms. Consideration should be made for the level of training, type of firearm, and environment. How much ear protection do I need for shooting? Outdoor: Minimum NRR 22. Indoor: NRR 28+ (preferably doubled). The more hazardous the environment, the higher the protection required. Can shooting damage hearing with ear protection? Yes, if your protection is insufficient for the noise level or not worn correctly. Damage can also occur if hearing protection is unintentionally moved out of place during live-fire training or competition. Are electronic ear muffs worth it? Absolutely. They allow you to hear conversations and commands while still protecting your hearing. They also provide next-gen options like text and phone call communications, as well as music playback (not recommended during live-fire training). The Axil MXII Pro covers all of the needs for recreational and competition shooting and is used around the world by experienced shooters needing optimal performance and protection. Conclusion Choosing the best ear protection for shooting has different factors, but matching your gear to your environment should be heavily considered. Indoor ranges → maximum protection (double up) Outdoor shooting → balance protection and awareness Competition/tactical → prioritize communication and mobility Modern options — especially electronic hearing protection like the Axil MXII or the XCOR Pro — make it easier than ever to stay safe without sacrificing performance. Having the best ear protection for the job allows shooters to maximize training value and optimize performance in competition. For professionals in law enforcement the stakes can be much higher. The information in this guide can assist all levels of shooters make the best decision to cover their needs and ensure the best protection, regardless of the environment.

articles.summary: A close-range firework can reach up to 150 to 175 decibels, louder than a jet engine at takeoff and well above the level that causes immediate hearing damage in unprotected ears. The question many parents ask first when it comes to fireworks is simple: how loud are fireworks? The answer is that they are among the loudest sounds most families will experience all year. Whether you're attending a backyard Fourth of July display, a professional fireworks show, a New Year's Eve celebration, or Disney fireworks, the noise levels routinely exceed what hearing experts consider safe without protection. This guide covers: How loud fireworks are in decibels Whether babies and kids need hearing protection The best ear protection for adults, toddlers, and infants Dog ear protection during fireworks NRR ratings and what they actually mean Why AirPods are not hearing protection How to protect your family's hearing during fireworks season AXIL has spent more than a decade designing and manufacturing hearing protection for shooters, NASCAR fans, industrial workers, and concert-goers. Fireworks create a similar challenge: protecting ears from intense impulse noise while remaining comfortable enough to wear through an entire event. How Loud Are Fireworks? The Decibel Reality Professional fireworks typically measure between 150 and 175 decibels at the launch site, while consumer fireworks often peak between 140 and 160 decibels. That places fireworks in the same category as: Gunshots Jet engines Professional racing environments Industrial impulse-noise events Why Are Fireworks So Loud? Fireworks create a rapid chemical explosion inside a confined shell. When that pressure is released, it creates a powerful shockwave that travels through the air. This explosive impulse is why fireworks often sound louder than other sounds with comparable decibel ratings. How Loud Are Fireworks From a Distance? Distance helps, but not as much as many people think. Distance From Launch Approximate dB Level Launch Site 150–175 dB 50 Feet 130–140 dB 200 Feet 110–125 dB 500 Feet 100–110 dB 1,000 Feet 95–105 dB Even at 1,000 feet, prolonged exposure can exceed safe listening thresholds. OSHA and NIOSH both recognize that sustained exposure above safe noise levels can contribute to cumulative and progressive hearing damage. Fireworks vs Other Loud Sounds Sound Approximate dB Conversation 60 dB Rock Concert 110–130 dB Thunder 110–120 dB Fireworks 140–175 dB 12-Gauge Shotgun 145–165 dB Centerfire Rifle 150–175 dB Jet Engine (100 ft) 140+ dB Are Fireworks Louder Than Gunshots? Not necessarily. A centerfire rifle and a professional firework shell can produce similar peak decibel levels. The difference is that a fireworks show can expose you to hundreds of impulse events in a single evening, which increases cumulative exposure. Can Fireworks Cause Permanent Hearing Damage? Yes. Fireworks can cause permanent hearing damage when exposure occurs without adequate hearing protection. Signs of overexposure to hazardous noise include: Ringing ears (tinnitus) Muffled hearing Ear discomfort Difficulty understanding speech after the event Children may not recognize or communicate these symptoms, which is one reason hearing protection is especially important for younger attendees. Are Fireworks Too Loud for Babies, Kids and Newborns? Yes. Fireworks are too loud for babies, newborns, and toddlers without hearing protection. A child's hearing system is still developing, and younger children are particularly vulnerable to impulse noise exposure, particularly for long periods. Age-by-Age Fireworks Hearing Protection Guide Newborn (0–6 mo) Avoid fireworks shows if possible Infant (6–12 mo) NRR 25+ earmuffs Toddler (1–3 yrs) NRR 22–27 earmuffs Child (4–12 yrs) NRR 22–27 earmuffs Teen Adult-rated protection Are Fireworks Too Loud for a 3-Month-Old? Absolutely. Most pediatric hearing experts recommend avoiding public fireworks displays with very young infants whenever possible. If attendance is unavoidable: Use infant-specific earmuffs Stay 500+ feet away Leave immediately if the baby becomes distressed Does My 1-Year-Old Need Ear Protection for Fireworks? Without question. One-year-olds and toddlers should wear properly fitted hearing protection throughout the event. Adult earmuffs generally do not seal properly on a toddler's head and often provide significantly less protection than advertised. What About Pregnancy? Many OB-GYNs recommend maintaining distance from launch areas during late pregnancy. While maternal hearing protection primarily protects the mother, avoiding close-range exposure and maintaining distance from launch sites is generally considered prudent.
